title-group.article-title: Foreign Assistance and Power-Sector Carbon Emissions in the MENA Region: The Roles of Trade, Foreign Direct Investment, and Foreign Development Assistance

abstract.p: Foreign assistance may help reduce power-sector carbon emissions (PSCE). This study examines the effect of net official development assistance and official aid (NODAOA) on PSCE in 16 Middle East and North Africa (MENA) economies over the period 1985–2024, within the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) framework. Foreign direct investment (FDI) and trade openness (TO) are included as control variables. PSCE is measured as CO2 emissions from electricity and heat production. Given the expected spatial linkages among geographically proximate MENA economies, the study applies a Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) to examine spatial dependence and spillover effects. The results support the EKC hypothesis, although 14 of the 16 MENA economies remain in its first phase. This suggests that economic growth has not yet been accompanied by a reduction in PSCE in most of the sampled economies. NODAOA is negatively associated with emissions through significant direct and spillover effects, highlighting the potential role of development assistance in supporting cleaner electricity transitions. By contrast, FDI is positively associated with PSCE across the estimated specifications, whereas the effect of TO is statistically insignificant. These findings highlight the challenge of coordinating regional decarbonization pathways in fossil-fuel-dependent MENA economies. They also identify development assistance as a potential channel for improving the environmental performance of the power sector, in line with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 7 and 13.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The power sector accounts for approximately 40% of energy-related carbon emissions (Bhattacharyya et al., 2018). The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region has some of the world’s most abundant solar and wind resources. Nevertheless, power-sector carbon emissions (PSCE) in the region have more than doubled since 2000, exceeding 950 million tons in 2023 (World Bank, 2026). Natural gas-fired generation accounts for approximately 65% of regional power-sector emissions, while oil-fired generation contributes about 30% (Akadiri & Olanipekun, 2025). Against this background, external economic and financial linkages, including trade openness (TO), foreign direct investment (FDI), and net official development assistance and official aid (NODAOA), may support energy transitions by providing the capital, technology, infrastructure, and expertise required for this transformation (Ebaidalla, 2025; Gafsi, 2025; Hanni et al., 2011). Understanding how TO, FDI, and NODAOA are associated with PSCE is therefore important for addressing the region’s sustainability challenges. MENA power systems remain heavily dependent on oil and natural gas. Accordingly, regional decarbonization requires coordinated transition pathways across increasingly interconnected electricity markets. This study contributes to this agenda by examining how external financial and trade flows are associated with the environmental performance of the MENA power sector.

The environmental consequences of TO, FDI, and NODAOA are not necessarily beneficial. Trade, for example, can increase energy demand and reinforce dependence on fossil fuels through scale effects (Roshid et al., 2026). However, it may also facilitate the diffusion of renewable-energy technologies and energy-efficiency equipment (Wiredu et al., 2025). Similarly, FDI may facilitate the transfer of cleaner production technologies and managerial expertise (Kiliçarslan, 2019). Conversely, it may reinforce carbon-intensive infrastructure and extractive industrial structures (Hanni et al., 2011). Foreign assistance, by comparison, is often directed toward energy and climate objectives and may therefore support low-carbon transitions and emissions reductions (Sharma et al., 2019). Its effectiveness, however, depends on governance quality, absorptive capacity, and alignment between donor and recipient priorities (Sharma et al., 2019; Shuyue & Yue, 2025).

In the power sector, trade may either increase or reduce PSCE. For example, trade may stimulate export-oriented industrialization in petrochemicals, aluminium, steel, cement, and other electricity-intensive industries in many MENA economies. Revenues from hydrocarbon exports may also support investment in conventional electricity infrastructure. These mechanisms are consistent with the Pollution Haven Hypothesis, which suggests that trade may delay the renewable-energy transition in economies with carbon-intensive industrial structures (Akadiri & Olanipekun, 2025; Bellakhal et al., 2019). Conversely, trade may improve access to renewable-energy technologies and energy-efficient electricity infrastructure (Groba & Cao, 2015; Zhu et al., 2022). It may also increase competition in electricity markets, potentially supporting renewable-energy deployment and market efficiency (Brekke et al., 2025).

FDI may also influence PSCE. In MENA economies, FDI is often directed toward the hydrocarbon sector, which may contribute to higher emissions. It may also promote energy-intensive manufacturing, increasing electricity demand and fossil-fuel-based generation. The Pollution Haven Hypothesis suggests that FDI can relocate pollution-intensive production to countries with relatively weak environmental compliance requirements, potentially delaying the renewable-energy transition in recipient economies (Kiliçarslan, 2019; Ouyang & Li, 2024). Conversely, FDI may introduce smart-grid systems, renewable-energy infrastructure, and improved operating practices that increase electricity efficiency and reduce carbon intensity. For example, greenfield investment in solar, wind, hydropower, and energy storage can expand renewable electricity capacity and potentially reduce PSCE (Kushawaha, 2025).

The effect of NODAOA on PSCE depends partly on the type of electricity infrastructure that the assistance finances. If allocated to conventional electricity infrastructure, NODAOA may increase PSCE. Alternatively, it may support renewable infrastructure by financing solar, wind, and hydropower projects, electricity-grid modernization, smart-grid technologies, energy storage, and energy-efficiency improvements (Sharma et al., 2019). Such investments may reduce PSCE. NODAOA may also provide technical assistance to strengthen energy governance (Chapel, 2022), potentially supporting renewable-energy expansion and reducing emissions. The literature therefore suggests that the environmental effects of NODAOA depend on donor priorities, governance quality, and project composition (Huang & Uddin, 2025; Salakpi et al., 2025).

The relationships among trade, FDI, NODAOA, and PSCE may also involve spatial linkages in MENA economies. Trade integration, for example, may facilitate cross-border flows of electricity-generation technologies, including both renewable and fossil-fuel-based technologies. Consequently, PSCE may depend not only on domestic environmental standards but also on the environmental standards, technology adoption, and trade policies of trading partners and neighboring economies (Groba & Cao, 2015; Maydybura et al., 2024). FDI may similarly facilitate the diffusion of clean technologies and managerial expertise when investment is directed toward renewable-energy projects (Chen et al., 2021; Henderson & Sommer, 2022; Mendler-Krakau & Frenkel, 2026; Xiahou et al., 2022). Regional foreign investment may therefore either facilitate or hinder the renewable-energy transition through spatial spillovers. NODAOA may also operate through spatial channels. For instance, renewable-energy assistance may generate positive spillovers through regional power pools and grid-interconnection projects (Wu et al., 2021). Conversely, assistance for fossil-fuel projects may reinforce carbon lock-in across the region (Bertheau & Lindner, 2022; Bhattacharyya et al., 2018; Chapel, 2022; Tirpak & Adams, 2008).

Figure 1 shows the average spatial distribution of PSCE across MENA economies over the period 1985–2024. The first cluster comprises Algeria, Morocco, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, and Tunisia, which record relatively low PSCE levels of less than 29.645 million tonnes of CO2 (Mt CO2). Oman, Qatar, and Bahrain also fall within this low-emissions group. The second cluster includes Egypt, Iraq, Israel, Kuwait, and the UAE, with moderate PSCE levels ranging from 29.645 to 52.77 Mt CO2. Saudi Arabia and Iran record the highest and second-highest levels, at 145.28 and 102.72 Mt CO2, respectively. Overall, the geographical distribution of PSCE provides a rationale for the formal spatial-dependence tests reported in Section 4. The class intervals in Figure 1 were determined using the natural-breaks method. The map is descriptive and does not, by itself, establish spatial dependence. Formal evidence is therefore provided by the Moran’s I and Lagrange Multiplier tests reported in Section 4.

sec.p: A growing body of literature examines the environmental effects of TO, FDI, and NODAOA. However, previous studies have focused mainly on aggregate carbon emissions (Bhattacharyya et al., 2018; Henderson & Sommer, 2022; Maydybura et al., 2024), ecological footprints (Roshid et al., 2026), or renewable-energy consumption and the renewable-energy transition (Akadiri & Olanipekun, 2025; Gafsi, 2025; Murshed, 2018; Salakpi et al., 2025; Wiredu et al., 2025). Sector-specific analyses remain limited globally, and research on the NODAOA–PSCE relationship in the MENA region is particularly scarce. Examining the power sector is important because electricity generation is a major source of global pollution (Bhattacharyya et al., 2018). Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, no previous study has examined the effect of NODAOA on PSCE in MENA economies using spatial analysis. Spatial linkages are plausible in the region because of integrated trade, cross-border investment, electricity interconnections, and shared energy infrastructure. Ignoring these spillovers may lead to biased estimates of the relationships between TO, FDI, NODAOA, and PSCE in MENA economies.

These research gaps motivate this study’s examination of the effects of TO, FDI, and NODAOA on PSCE in 16 MENA economies over the period 1985–2024, within the EKC framework and using spatial econometric techniques. The study contributes methodologically by applying the Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) to distinguish between the direct and spillover effects of TO, FDI, and NODAOA on PSCE. Empirically, it extends the EKC literature by examining power-sector emissions rather than aggregate emissions and by jointly assessing the roles of TO, FDI, and NODAOA. From a policy perspective, the estimated direct and spillover effects provide evidence on whether NODAOA and FDI are associated with decarbonization or carbon-intensive activity in the MENA power sector. The findings can inform coordinated regional transition strategies aligned with SDGs 7 and 13.

sec.title: 2. Literature review
sec.p: The electricity sector is a major source of global energy-related emissions. Understanding the determinants of PSCE is therefore important for climate-change mitigation. This study focuses on three external determinants: FDI, TO, and NODAOA. The following subsections review the literature on these factors and their potential roles in power-sector decarbonization.

sec.title: 2.1. Trade and the energy market
sec.p: Trade may facilitate access to renewable-energy equipment, energy-efficiency technologies, and advanced generating systems. These channels can support low-carbon electricity generation through technological effects (Groba & Cao, 2015; Zhao et al., 2016). However, trade expansion may also increase electricity demand through scale effects, particularly in industrialized economies and those specializing in energy-intensive goods. This may encourage carbon-intensive production (Akadiri & Olanipekun, 2025; Roshid et al., 2026).

Akadiri & Olanipekun (2025) used quantile regression for 13 MENA countries over 2001–2023 and found that TO increased dependence on fossil fuels, thereby constraining the renewable-energy transition. However, oil rents and TO jointly promoted renewable-energy adoption. Bellakhal et al. (2019) examined 16 MENA countries over 1996–2013 and found that better governance promoted the renewable-energy transition, with TO having a moderating effect. Murshed (2018) examined the effects of TO on the renewable-energy transition in five Asian economies over 2000–2017 and found that TO improved renewable-energy consumption, energy efficiency, and access to clean-cooking technologies. Zhu et al. (2022) investigated mineral-trade networks over 2000–2019 and found that these networks and trade promoted renewable-energy deployment in high-income economies. Zhao et al. (2016) analyzed the effect of TO on China’s exports of 62 renewable-energy products to 116 economies over 2000–2012. They found that TO encouraged renewable-energy exports and that tariff reductions facilitated entry into export markets, increasing the volume of renewable-energy product trade. This effect was more pronounced among foreign-owned exporting firms. Wiredu et al. (2025) examined NAFTA economies over 1990–2020 and found positive relationships among economic advancement, digital-technology adoption, and TO, which jointly supported the renewable-energy transition. However, population growth and urbanization weakened this effect by increasing energy demand.

Carbon emissions trading (CET) systems have been identified as policy instruments for managing power-sector emissions. Liu et al. (2023) examined the power industry in 30 Chinese provinces over 2010–2019 and found that CET reduced emissions in the sector. Public spending and per capita gross domestic product (GDP) also reduced emissions. Lessmann & Kramer (2024) studied the effect of CET on the US power sector over 2005–2019 and found that it reduced PSCE. Using data from Guangdong, Kim et al. (2026) examined regulated Chinese electricity forward markets and found that tradable performance standards reduced carbon emissions. Rui et al. (2023) investigated hybrid renewable-energy systems and concluded that the grandfathering mechanism improved firms’ utilization efficiency in renewable-energy power production. Shuyue & Yue (2025) examined CET and renewable-energy support policies in the Chinese power sector during electricity-market reform. They found that CET was the most effective mitigation mechanism, although its effectiveness was weakened by renewable-energy support policies that were associated with higher emissions. Tumusiime & Li (2026) investigated China’s CET system over 2008–2022 and found that it increased total-factor power-generation efficiency; environmental resource commitment accounted for 25% of the gains. Rego et al. (2025) examined socially oriented energy trading in Portuguese renewable-energy communities and found that it reduced CO2 emissions.

The literature indicates that trade can increase electricity demand and reinforce fossil-fuel dependence through scale effects. Conversely, it can facilitate access to renewable-energy equipment and energy-efficiency technologies through technique effects. The net effect of trade is therefore uncertain, particularly in the MENA region, where trade remains heavily concentrated in hydrocarbons. This study addresses this uncertainty by estimating the direct and spillover effects of TO on PSCE in 16 MENA economies.

sec.title: 2.2. Foreign direct investment and the energy market
sec.p: The relationship between FDI and PSCE may operate through either the Pollution Haven Hypothesis or the pollution-halo hypothesis. The Pollution Haven Hypothesis suggests that FDI may relocate carbon-intensive electricity generation to regions with weaker environmental enforcement, thereby increasing PSCE (Henderson & Sommer, 2022; Maydybura et al., 2024). Conversely, the pollution-halo hypothesis proposes that FDI can transfer cleaner technologies, improve environmental management practices, and introduce more efficient production methods, thereby reducing emissions intensity and supporting the renewable-energy transition (Kiliçarslan, 2019; Xiahou et al., 2022).

In a sector-specific analysis, Chen et al. (2021) used data on overseas power-generation finance from 2000–2018 and found that financing commitments were concentrated in fossil-fuel technologies: 64% in China, 87% in Japan, and 66% in the United States. They associated overseas fossil-fuel power financing with carbon-lock-in risks in the power sector. Blackman & Wu (1999) investigated China’s power sector and found that FDI improved energy efficiency through the adoption of advanced generating technologies. Technology transfer therefore reduced the carbon intensity of fossil-fuel generation. Xiahou et al. (2022) examined the environmental performance of 2,108 Asian coal-fired power plants and found that foreign-funded plants were 3.4% cleaner than domestically funded plants. Improved technology accounted for 96% of this difference. Mendler-Krakau & Frenkel (2026) examined Chinese official finance to Africa over 2000–2021 and found that it supported greener electricity generation. Tao et al. (2025) assessed 203 overseas renewable-energy power systems receiving Chinese investment and found that Chinese FDI was directed toward countries with weaker legal frameworks, where environmental improvements were smaller.

Kiliçarslan (2019) examined the BRICS economies over 1996–2015 and found that FDI did not improve renewable-energy production. By contrast, Aggarwal & Mahalik (2026) analyzed Asian economies over 1996–2020 and found that FDI increased renewable-energy productivity. Effective governance also enhanced renewable-energy productivity. Kushawaha (2025) examined 41 developing countries over 2003–2022 and reported a U-shaped relationship between greenfield FDI and renewable-energy capacity. Mergers and acquisitions involving FDI, as well as public debt, also had positive effects on renewable-energy capacity. Rashed et al. (2022) investigated FDI in renewable electricity in 32 African countries over 2003–2019 and found that it supported renewable-electricity development. Salakpi et al. (2025) examined globalization and renewable-energy consumption in Sub-Saharan Africa over 1995–2022 and found that globalization increased renewable-energy consumption. Economic globalization supported renewable-energy consumption through trade and FDI, social globalization facilitated knowledge spillovers, and political globalization promoted international cooperation and policy alignment in renewable-energy adoption.

Ouyang & Li (2024) reported that institutional distance between developed and developing countries had a negative effect on renewable-energy investment over 2009–2018. However, renewable-energy policies moderated this relationship. The negative association between institutional distance and renewable-energy investment was weaker in developing countries where FDI was directed toward renewable-energy generation. Ebaidalla (2025) examined 88 developing countries over 1996–2020 and found that migrant remittances increased both renewable-energy consumption and renewable-energy production. FDI also had a positive effect on renewable-energy production, although it did not increase renewable-energy consumption. Hanni et al. (2011) analyzed FDI in renewable-electricity generation over 2003–2010 and found that governance strengthened the effect of FDI on renewable-energy investment, as governments used FDI as a source of external climate finance. Maydybura et al. (2024) examined 30 Chinese industries over 2001–2024 and found nonlinear relationships between FDI, TO, and sectoral carbon emissions. FDI and TO reduced emissions at lower emission thresholds but increased them at higher thresholds.

The literature presents contrasting findings. Some studies suggest that FDI relocates carbon-intensive generation, consistent with the Pollution Haven Hypothesis, whereas others find that FDI facilitates the transfer of cleaner technologies, consistent with the pollution-halo hypothesis. This disagreement may persist because sector-specific FDI allocations are rarely observed. Consequently, it remains uncertain whether FDI in MENA economies is directed primarily toward fossil-fuel or renewable electricity generation. This study therefore estimates the net association between FDI and PSCE in the MENA region without assuming either hypothesis in advance.

sec.title: 2.3. Foreign assistance and the energy market
sec.p: Foreign assistance is an important channel through which international financial flows may influence domestic energy markets and PSCE in developing and emerging economies. Foreign assistance can support energy infrastructure and climate-mitigation technologies by financing renewable-energy projects and infrastructure modernization (Bhattacharyya et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021). However, its effectiveness in reducing PSCE depends on governance quality, absorptive capacity, and donor priorities (Barkat et al., 2024; Kablan & Chouard, 2022; Henderson & Sommer, 2022).

Bhattacharyya et al. (2018) examined 128 countries over 1971–2011 and found that energy-related foreign assistance reduced emissions only in Europe and Central Asia, indicating regional variation in its effectiveness. Henderson & Sommer (2022) found that development assistance increased CO2 emissions in a panel of 122 economies, highlighting the potential role of foreign assistance in reinforcing fossil-fuel dependence. Conversely, Barkat et al. (2024) examined 127 developing countries over 1995–2019 and found that foreign assistance reduced carbon emissions, primarily through direct green-investment channels. The effect also varied with income: foreign assistance had a limited effect in low-income economies but a stronger effect in middle-income countries.

The literature has also examined climate- and energy-related assistance. Kablan & Chouard (2022) investigated whether climate aid accelerated renewable-energy adoption and reduced CO2 emissions in recipient countries. They found that climate aid for renewable-energy had only a limited effect on emissions reduction, suggesting that developing countries may prioritize economic efficiency over environmental efficiency. However, climate aid had a significant emissions-reducing effect in economies with a carbon tax. They also found that FDI facilitated the import of environmentally beneficial technologies and reduced emissions. Wu et al. (2021) analyzed 52 recipient countries over 1980–2016 and concluded that climate aid reduced emissions by supporting the substitution of clean energy for fossil fuels and facilitating the renewable-energy transition in recipient economies.

Bertheau & Lindner (2022) examined energy-related assistance in Southeast Asian economies and found that it supported fossil-fuel power-generation projects, highlighting a gap between donor climate commitments and actual aid-allocation patterns. Sharma et al. (2019) investigated Nepal and reported that foreign assistance and remittances reduced CO2 emissions, whereas financial development and income increased them. Chapel (2022) examined 19 Sub-Saharan African countries and found that renewable-energy assistance supported renewable-electrification projects. Li et al. (2024) examined African economies and concluded that targeted official development assistance for renewable-energy reduced ecological pressures.

Overall, the literature reports mixed findings. Some studies find that energy-related assistance reduces emissions, whereas others show that foreign assistance may reinforce fossil-fuel dependence. It therefore remains uncertain whether foreign assistance reduces PSCE in MENA economies and whether its effects extend across national borders. The present study examines both questions.

sec.title: 2.4. Literature gap and contribution of the study
sec.p: The reviewed literature shows that most previous studies have focused on national-level environmental indicators. Sector-specific analyses, particularly of the power sector, remain limited, despite electricity generation being a major source of global emissions. Studies that jointly examine the effects of trade, FDI, and foreign assistance are also scarce. In particular, the effects of these factors on PSCE have not been adequately investigated in the MENA region. This study addresses these gaps by examining their relationships with PSCE using spatial econometric methods. Spatial analysis is appropriate given the geographical proximity of MENA economies and the potential for cross-border spillovers arising from interconnected electricity markets, regional energy trade, shared fossil-fuel resources, common renewable-energy initiatives, and the transboundary nature of environmental pressures. The study provides new empirical evidence and policy-relevant insights into low-carbon transitions in the power sectors of fossil-fuel-dependent MENA economies.

sec.title: 3. Methodology
sec.p: The relationship between NODAOA and PSCE must be considered alongside the role of economic growth. Grossman & Krueger (1995) proposed a nonlinear relationship between economic growth and environmental indicators, known as the EKC. In the early stages of development, industrialization and rising living standards may increase economic activity, electricity demand, and PSCE, particularly in MENA countries where electricity generation relies heavily on fossil fuels. At higher income levels, however, structural transformation, technological progress, and stronger environmental regulation may reduce PSCE as demand for environmental quality increases, potentially decoupling emissions from economic growth (Stern, 2004). Similarly, Abrell & Rausch (2016) argued that higher-income economies may adopt renewable-energy, improve grid efficiency, and retire carbon-intensive plants through technological innovation. An inverted U-shaped relationship between PSCE and economic growth is therefore expected.

This study extends the EKC framework by incorporating NODAOA, FDI, and TO as external factors that may shape the relationship between income and power-sector emissions. NODAOA may support power-sector decarbonization when directed toward renewable-energy infrastructure, including renewable generation, transmission modernization, and grid integration (Bhattacharyya et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021). FDI may also reduce PSCE when invested in renewable electricity generation. Conversely, investment in fossil-fuel projects may create carbon-intensive infrastructure (Chen et al., 2021; Mendler-Krakau & Frenkel, 2026). TO may affect PSCE through both scale and technique effects. Trade expansion may increase electricity demand and fossil-fuel dependence in resource-rich MENA economies. However, trade may also improve access to renewable-energy equipment, energy-efficiency technologies, and innovation spillovers (Akadiri & Olanipekun, 2025; Groba & Cao, 2015; Murshed, 2018), potentially reducing PSCE. The subscript t denotes the year, covering 1985–2024. PSCEit is the natural logarithm of CO2 emissions from electricity and heat production, measured in million tonnes of CO2 (Mt CO2). GDPCit is the natural logarithm of GDP per capita (constant 2015 USD), and GDPCit2 is the square of GDPCit. FDIit denotes net foreign direct investment inflows as a percentage of GDP. TOit is the natural logarithm of total trade as a percentage of GDP. NODAOAit is the natural logarithm of net official development assistance and official aid received, measured in billions of constant 2023 USD. All data were obtained from the World Development Indicators (World Bank, 2026). To obtain a complete panel for 1985–2024, missing observations (9.6%) within the observed period were estimated using linear interpolation. Missing values outside the observed period were estimated using linear extrapolation. NODAOAit is used as the empirical proxy for foreign assistance because it is the most consistently reported cross-country measure of development finance and is available annually for all 16 sample economies. It comprises bilateral and multilateral concessional flows and official aid. However, it also includes flows not specifically directed toward the energy or power sector. Therefore, NODAOAit captures the broader development-finance environment rather than assistance targeted specifically at the power sector.

Eq. (1) was estimated using pooled ordinary least squares (POLS) and fixed effects (FE). Moran’s I, Lagrange Multiplier (LM), and robust LM tests were then applied to detect spatial effects in the POLS and FE estimates (Elhorst, 2014). If these tests indicate significant spatial effects, non-spatial POLS and FE estimates may be biased because they omit spatial spillovers. Spatial dependence in PSCEit is plausible among MENA economies because of their geographical proximity and shared fossil-fuel endowments. It may also arise from interconnected energy infrastructure, cross-border electricity trade, common energy policies, and the diffusion of energy technologies across neighboring economies (LeSage & Pace, 2009). Changes in electricity generation or decarbonization policies in one MENA economy may therefore be associated with spillover effects in neighboring economies.

These considerations justify the use of spatial econometric models to account for regional interdependence rather than relying solely on non-spatial estimation techniques. Accordingly, the Spatial Autoregressive (SAR), Spatial Error Model (SEM), and SDM were applied to Eq. (1). The Wald test was used to determine whether the SDM could be reduced to the SEM or SAR (Anselin, 1988). The results were then used to identify the most appropriate spatial specification. Eq. Given the small sample of 16 economies, a 4,500 km cutoff was adopted to define spatial neighborhoods and focus the analysis on geographically proximate economies. Spatial weights for country pairs separated by more than 4,500 km were therefore set to zero to exclude distant economies and capture potentially meaningful spatial interactions. The matrix was row-normalized by dividing each element by its row sum (Kelejian & Prucha, 2010). Higher inverse-distance weights indicate greater geographical proximity and, potentially, a greater likelihood of spatial interaction. Thus, the coefficient of W × PSCEit represents the spatial lag of PSCEit. The β11, …, β15 terms are regression coefficients of the explanatory variables; the estimated regression coefficients are not, by themselves, average direct or indirect effects. The average direct effects are impact measures derived from the reduced-form spatial multiplier. The impact measures are calculated from the matrix of partial derivatives of the reduced form, as explained in Section 4. (4) specifies 𝜀2it as spatially autoregressive with respect to the weight matrix W. Spatial dependence is therefore captured by λ1, which indicates that the residual structure reflects shocks associated across MENA economies. Finally, the SDM is specified as follows:

The coefficient ρ2 captures spatial dependence in PSCEit among MENA economies through the spatially lagged dependent variable. The coefficients β31, …, β35 represent the spatial lags of the explanatory variables, while β41, …, β45 enter the reduced-form spatial multiplier. Neither set of coefficients should be interpreted directly as average direct or indirect effects; these are impact measures derived from the reduced-form spatial multiplier. To test the robustness of Eq. (5), the inverse-distance spatial weight matrix was replaced with a contiguity-based matrix. This matrix assigns a value of 1 to countries sharing a land border and 0 otherwise. Because Bahrain has no land-border neighbor in the sample, Saudi Arabia was assigned as its nearest neighbor based on great-circle distance, and a binary spatial weight of 1 was assigned to this link. This treatment is also geographically justified by the physical connection between the two countries via the King Fahd Causeway. The resulting matrix was row-standardized by dividing each nonzero element by its corresponding row sum, so that the weights in each row summed to one.

sec.title: 4. Results
sec.p: Table 1 presents the correlation matrix. PSCEit is positively correlated with GDPCit, FDIit, and TOit, suggesting that economic growth, FDI, and TO may be associated with higher PSCE. By contrast, NODAOAit is negatively correlated with PSCEit, suggesting a possible association between development assistance and lower power-sector emissions. The correlations among the explanatory variables are relatively low. The highest correlation is observed between FDIit and TOit, both of which reflect aspects of external economic integration. Overall, the relatively low correlations suggest that multicollinearity is unlikely to pose a serious concern in the estimated model.

Table 2 shows that GDPCit and GDPCit2 have positive and negative coefficients, respectively, across all estimated non-spatial specifications, supporting an EKC relationship between economic growth and PSCE in the MENA region. FDIit is positively associated with PSCEit, whereas NODAOAit is negatively associated with it. The estimated effect of TOit is statistically insignificant. The spatial diagnostic tests show that Moran’s I, LM, and robust LM statistics are statistically significant at the 1% level, indicating the presence of spatial-lag and spatial-error dependence across the estimated specifications. Spatial-error dependence suggests that omitted shocks affecting PSCE in one MENA country may also be associated with outcomes in neighboring countries. Spatial-lag dependence further indicates that PSCE in one country is associated with emissions patterns in nearby countries. The non-spatial models may therefore provide unreliable estimates because the data exhibit spatial dependence, which violates the assumption of cross-sectional independence. Accordingly, the analysis proceeds with spatial estimation of the hypothesized model.

As shown in Table 3, the Wald tests for the spatial lag and spatial error components are highly significant in both the FE and RE models, indicating that the SDM cannot be reduced to either the SEM or the SAR. The SDM is therefore the most appropriate spatial specification for the hypothesized model. The Hausman test is also statistically significant and favors the SDM with FE. Accordingly, the conclusions are based on the SDM-FE estimates. Because the SDM includes both spatially lagged regressors and a spatially lagged dependent variable, the coefficients of the spatially lagged regressors cannot be interpreted directly as marginal effects. Instead, direct, indirect, and total effects are calculated from the reduced form of the model, following LeSage & Pace (2009). Direct effects capture the effects of changes in a country’s own regressors, whereas indirect effects capture effects associated with changes in neighboring countries’ regressors. Total effects are the sum of the direct and indirect effects.

The direct effects of GDPCit and GDPCit2 on PSCEit are positive and negative, respectively, supporting the EKC hypothesis, with an estimated turning point of USD 55,719 in constant prices. Based on observed GDP per capita values (constant USD 712–81,608) across the sample, Qatar exceeded this threshold during 2004–2024, while the UAE exceeded it during 1985–1998, in 2000, and in 2006. The remaining sample economies did not reach the threshold during the study period. This suggests that, below the turning point, increases in GDP per capita are associated with higher PSCE in most sample economies. FDIit has a positive direct effect on PSCEit. This association is consistent with a scale effect, whereby foreign investment expands economic activity and electricity demand. However, the data do not identify the sectoral allocation of FDI, so this interpretation is suggestive rather than conclusive. FDI inflows to MENA economies may be directed toward hydrocarbon activities, including carbon-intensive oil and gas production. Given the region’s reliance on fossil-fuel-based electricity generation, increased electricity demand associated with FDI may also be reflected in higher PSCE. NODAOAit has a negative direct effect on PSCEit. This association may reflect support for renewable electricity, grid modernization, and technical assistance through development assistance. However, because the aggregate NODAOA measure does not identify funding allocated specifically to the power sector, this interpretation should also be treated as suggestive. TOit has a positive but statistically insignificant direct effect on PSCEit.

caption.title: SDM estimates based on the inverse-distance matrix

sec.p: All spatially weighted regressors, except W × TOit, have statistically significant coefficients. This indicates that the characteristics of neighboring countries are associated with a country’s PSCE. The coefficient of W × PSCEit is also positive, suggesting that PSCE in one MENA economy is spatially associated with higher PSCE in neighboring economies.

The estimated indirect effects of GDPCit and GDPCit2 are positive and negative, respectively. The positive indirect effect of GDPCit indicates that economic growth in one MENA country is associated with higher PSCE in neighboring countries. This relationship may reflect regional energy-market linkages, common fuel-supply structures, and cross-border power-sector infrastructure. The negative indirect effect of GDPCit2 suggests that the EKC-related decline in emissions beyond the turning point may also be reflected in neighboring economies. The indirect effect of FDIit is positive. This association may be consistent with competition among MENA economies for fossil-fuel investment, although the model does not directly estimate such competition. It may also reflect regional supply-chain integration, investment clustering, or shared electricity-market pressures. The indirect effect of NODAOAit is negative, suggesting that development assistance in one country may be associated with environmental benefits in neighboring economies. Such spillovers may operate through donor-led regional initiatives and cross-border infrastructure, although these channels are not separately measured in the model.

The total effects are the sum of the direct and indirect effects and therefore represent the overall effects of the explanatory variables on regional PSCE. GDPCit and GDPCit2 have positive and negative total effects, respectively, supporting the EKC hypothesis for the MENA power sector when both domestic effects and spatial spillovers are considered. The estimated turning point is USD 53,854 in constant prices. Based on annual GDP per capita values over 1985–2024, Qatar exceeded this threshold during 2004–2024, while the UAE exceeded it during 1985–2001 and 2004–2006. The remaining sample economies remained in the first phase and did not reach the threshold. The total effect of FDIit is positive and statistically significant, indicating that FDI inflows are associated with higher PSCE across the MENA region. By contrast, NODAOAit has a negative and statistically significant total effect, suggesting that development assistance is associated with lower power-sector emissions overall. This result indicates that aid may support decarbonization through domestic improvements and cross-border spillovers. The total effect of TO is statistically insignificant.

Table 4 presents the SDM results based on the contiguity matrix, using the same sample of 16 MENA economies over 1985–2024. The Hausman test favors FE, while the Wald tests indicate that the SDM cannot be reduced to either the SAR or SEM specification. The SDM-FE results based on the contiguity matrix are broadly consistent with those obtained using the inverse-distance matrix, although some coefficient magnitudes and significance levels differ. For example, the direct-effect coefficients of GDPCit and FDIit in Table 4 are positive and significant at the 1% level, compared with significance at the 5% level in Table 3. This indicates stronger statistical evidence under the contiguity specification. Similarly, the coefficients of GDPCit and GDPCit2 for the indirect and total effects show stronger statistical significance in Table 4. The spatially weighted coefficients of W × GDPCit, W × GDPCit2, and W × FDIit are also more statistically significant under the contiguity specification. In particular, W × FDIit is significant only at the 10% level in Table 3 but at the 5% level in Table 4. The significance levels of the remaining coefficients are similar across the two tables. Overall, Table 4 supports the baseline findings in Table 3 regarding the signs of the estimated effects, although the strength of the statistical evidence for some effects depends on the spatial weighting matrix.

caption.title: SDM estimates based on the contiguity matrix

sec.p: To account for differences in electricity-sector development and foreign financial flows across the MENA region, the SDM-FE estimates for 2000–2024 in Table 5 are compared with the full-sample estimates for 1985–2024 in Table 3 and Table 4. The signs and statistical significance of the effects of economic growth, FDI, and NODAOA are generally consistent across the two periods and spatial weight matrices. The direct and total effects of FDI and NODAOA are slightly larger in absolute terms in the more recent period. However, the indirect effect of economic growth decreases under the inverse-distance matrix but increases under the contiguity matrix, while its direct and total effects are larger. Under the contiguity matrix, the statistical significance of all FDI effects improves, whereas the significance levels of the other variables remain unchanged. Under the inverse-distance matrix, the significance levels are mostly consistent with those in the full-sample estimates. These sub-period results suggest that the baseline findings for FDI, NODAOA, economic growth, and spatial spillovers remain broadly consistent during the more recent phase of MENA energy-market development.

sec.title: 5. Discussion
sec.p: From a sustainability perspective, the findings suggest that the transition to low-carbon electricity in MENA is not exclusively a domestic process. Cross-border financial and trade linkages are also associated with this transition, as reflected in the indirect effects of FDI, TO, and NODAOA. The EKC estimates and turning points indicate that economic growth is associated with higher PSCE in all sample economies except Qatar and the UAE. This pattern is consistent with the continued reliance of most MENA economies on oil- and gas-based electricity and heat production (Akadiri & Olanipekun, 2025). It may also reflect urban expansion, rising cooling demand, industrial activity, and grid development accompanying economic growth in the region. At higher income levels, however, PSCE may decline in Qatar and the UAE. The significant spillover effects of economic growth further suggest that growth in higher-income MENA economies may be associated with regional benefits through demonstration effects, policy learning, and technology diffusion to lower-income economies. This finding is consistent with Abrell & Rausch (2016), who showed that electricity infrastructure and renewable-energy penetration can generate cross-border spillovers through electricity trade.

FDI has a positive direct association with PSCE, and the estimated spillover effects are also positive. This finding is consistent with the MENA energy landscape, where electricity generation remains heavily dependent on oil and natural gas. However, the study does not identify the sectoral allocation of FDI, and the results therefore cannot establish that foreign investment is primarily directed toward fossil-fuel power projects. The literature also shows that FDI can reduce emissions when it finances smart grids, energy storage, and cleaner generation technologies (Kiliçarslan, 2019; Rashed et al., 2022). Chen et al. (2021), by contrast, found that FDI can support fossil-fuel technologies in recipient countries. Xiahou et al. (2022) also showed that efficiency improvements in foreign-funded power plants may be insufficient to offset the overall expansion of fossil-fuel electricity generation. Stronger governance and supportive energy policies may therefore be needed to direct FDI toward the renewable-energy sector (Bellakhal et al., 2019).

The findings indicate that NODAOA is associated with lower emissions in the regional power sector. The estimated spillover effects also suggest potential regional benefits. These results are consistent with studies finding that renewable-energy assistance reduces PSCE (Chapel, 2022), climate-related aid reduces emissions by financing clean energy (Wu et al., 2021), and climate assistance for renewable-energy contributes to emissions reductions (Kablan & Chouard, 2022). Other studies, however, report adverse environmental outcomes associated with foreign assistance (Bhattacharyya et al., 2018; Henderson & Sommer, 2022). Overall, the results suggest that NODAOA may support the transition to cleaner electricity systems and generate positive regional spillovers across MENA economies.

TO has no statistically significant association with PSCE in the preferred specification. Aggregate TO may be too broad to capture the environmental consequences of energy-related trade. MENA economies differ substantially in their dependence on hydrocarbon exports, imports of manufactured goods, and trade in renewable-energy technologies. The insignificant coefficient should therefore be interpreted cautiously; it does not imply that energy-related trade is environmentally neutral in the region. Theoretically, trade may increase electricity demand through industrial expansion and export-oriented production, raising emissions through the scale effect of fossil-fuel consumption (Akadiri & Olanipekun, 2025). However, TO may also facilitate the diffusion of renewable-energy technologies, energy-efficient equipment, and cleaner electricity infrastructure (Groba & Cao, 2015; Murshed, 2018), thereby reducing PSCE through the technique effect. The statistically insignificant net effect in this study may indicate that the scale effect offsets the expected technique effect of trade in the MENA region. For example, the potential environmental benefits of importing cleaner technologies may be offset by increased activity in energy- and carbon-intensive export industries in economies that remain dependent on fossil-fuel exports.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p: This study examined the effects of NODAOA on PSCE within the EKC framework for 16 MENA economies over 1985–2024, using an SDM. In the preferred SDM-FE specification, PSCE in one MENA economy was spatially associated with PSCE in neighboring economies. This indicates that power-sector emissions are related not only to domestic conditions but also to cross-border spatial dependence. The estimated impact measures also provide evidence consistent with the EKC relationship between PSCE and economic growth at the direct, indirect, and total levels. Based on the total effects, Qatar was in the second phase of the EKC during 2004–2024, while the UAE was in this phase during 1985–2001 and 2004–2006. The remaining sample economies were in the first phase. FDI was positively associated with PSCE in the direct, indirect, and total impact estimates of the preferred SDM-FE specification. This pattern is consistent with an association between FDI and carbon-intensive electricity expansion rather than a low-carbon transition in the MENA region. Conversely, NODAOA was negatively associated with PSCE in the direct and total impact estimates. Its indirect estimate was also negative but was not statistically significant in some specifications; it should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of a robust spillover effect. Overall, NODAOA may be a relevant channel for supporting cleaner infrastructure and power-sector decarbonization, although the observational design does not establish causality. Finally, TO had no statistically significant association with PSCE in the preferred SDM-FE specification. This result may reflect offsetting scale and technique effects of trade in the power sector. The study contributes to the empirical literature on the MENA power sector by showing that the growth–emissions relationship is not exclusively domestic but is also spatially interconnected across geographically proximate economies.

The results show that NODAOA is negatively associated with PSCE in the direct and total impact estimates. MENA governments could therefore consider strengthening partnerships with development agencies to expand assistance for power-sector decarbonization. However, because the indirect NODAOA estimate is not statistically significant in some specifications, policy recommendations should focus primarily on the direct and total associations rather than assuming a robust spillover channel. FDI is positively associated with PSCE in the preferred SDM-FE direct, indirect, and total estimates. This finding highlights the importance of applying and enforcing environmental standards for foreign investment, particularly in carbon-intensive power generation. The significant spatial dependence in PSCE also supports regional coordination. MENA economies could coordinate renewable-energy investments and harmonize electricity-market regulations to address cross-border environmental effects in the power sector. Although the estimated impact measures are consistent with the EKC, 14 MENA economies remain in its first phase. These countries could therefore complement economic-growth targets with supportive renewable-power-sector policies to limit the environmental pressures associated with growth.

The findings also point to policy measures that were not directly tested in the model. To reduce the potential environmental pressures associated with FDI, governments could offer fiscal incentives for investment in renewable energy, energy storage, and smart-grid systems. Although TO has no statistically significant association with PSCE in the preferred specification, MENA countries could seek to reduce their dependence on fossil-fuel-based trade and diversify their trade structures. Governments could also incorporate environmental provisions into regional and bilateral trade agreements to encourage trade in renewable-energy technologies and promote cross-border trade in electricity generated from renewable sources.

This study has several limitations. Data on renewable-oriented and fossil-fuel-oriented NODAOA, TO, and FDI specifically allocated to the power sector are not consistently available. Consequently, the analysis cannot identify the sectoral channels through which these variables are associated with PSCE. Future research could use power-sector-specific data on FDI, trade, and development assistance to examine these relationships in greater detail. The analysis also does not incorporate electricity-sector governance indicators, such as electricity-tariff reform, subsidy restructuring, or renewable-energy policy instruments. Further research could disaggregate foreign financial flows by sector and technology and incorporate electricity-governance variables to identify more precisely the channels through which external economic integration is associated with power-sector decarbonization.
